title: Python lists and tuples
text: Python lists are mutable sequences: elements can be replaced, appended, and removed. Tuples are immutable sequences: their element references cannot be reassigned after creation. A tuple can nevertheless contain a mutable object, such as a list, whose own contents can change. Both lists and tuples preserve element order, allow duplicate values, and support indexing. A tuple is hashable only when all its elements are hashable.

title: Python sets and membership
text: A Python set is an unordered collection of distinct hashable objects. Adding an existing member does not create a duplicate. Sets support membership tests, union, intersection, and difference. A set does not promise insertion order, indexing, or slicing. A frozenset is immutable; a regular set is mutable. Use a sequence when an interface needs ordered positions.

title: Python dictionary keys and order
text: A Python dictionary maps unique hashable keys to values. Dictionaries preserve insertion order, a language guarantee from Python 3.7 onward. Replacing a value for an existing key does not move that key; deleting a key and inserting it again places it at the end. Dictionary membership tests keys, not values. Lists cannot be dictionary keys because they are unhashable.

title: Python deque endpoint operations
text: collections.deque supports efficient appends and pops at either end. append adds on the right, appendleft adds on the left, pop removes on the right, and popleft removes on the left. Endpoint appends and pops have approximately O(1) performance. A list pop(0) incurs O(n) movement of remaining elements, so a deque is a suitable choice for a FIFO queue with frequent removal from the front.

title: HTTP no-cache and no-store
text: In an HTTP response, Cache-Control: no-cache allows storage but requires successful validation before a stored response can satisfy another request. Cache-Control: no-store tells caches not to store the response. Therefore no-cache does not mean 'never store'. The private response directive prevents storage by shared caches, while a private cache may store the response subject to other directives.

title: HTTP freshness lifetimes
text: The Cache-Control response directive max-age specifies a freshness lifetime in seconds. A stored response is fresh when its calculated current age is less than its freshness lifetime. For shared caches, s-maxage overrides max-age and Expires when determining freshness. Freshness depends on age, not simply on how long the local cache has held the response. Other directives and request conditions may still require validation.

title: HTTP ETag conditional validation
text: An ETag is a validator for a selected HTTP representation. A client can send a stored entity tag in If-None-Match on a conditional GET. If the selected representation's entity tag matches the supplied tag, the server can respond 304 Not Modified. A 304 response has no message content; it lets a cache update metadata and reuse a matching stored representation. A changed representation is normally returned with a successful response and its body.

title: HTTP Vary and cached variants
text: The Vary response field identifies request fields, beyond the method and target URI, that influenced selection of a representation. For a stored response with Vary: Accept-Language, a cache must account for Accept-Language when matching a later request to that response. Vary separates selected representations; it does not set a freshness lifetime or disable all storage. Vary: * always fails the matching test for reuse without forwarding.

title: Request rate and counting windows
text: For this benchmark, QPS means completed queries per second: completed query count divided by the measurement interval in seconds. If 2,400 queries complete in 60 seconds, mean throughput is 40 QPS. Offered arrival rate and completed throughput are different measurements when work queues or fails. A mean rate does not specify peak rate, latency percentiles, or concurrent requests. This counting convention must be stated when comparing reports.

title: Latency percentiles and throughput
text: Latency measures the time taken to serve a request; throughput measures completed work per unit time. A p95 latency threshold means approximately 95 percent of measured requests finish at or below that threshold, under the measurement system's percentile convention. A percentile is not the mean or maximum latency. A throughput figure alone does not establish a latency percentile, and systems with equal throughput can have different latency distributions.

title: Horizontal and vertical scaling
text: Horizontal scaling changes the number of instances that share work. Vertical scaling changes the resources of an instance, such as its CPU count or memory. Adding instances does not guarantee proportional throughput: a shared database bottleneck, contention, or uneven work distribution can limit gains. A measured workload and its bottleneck are needed to estimate an actual capacity improvement.

title: Little's law in a stable service
text: Little's law relates long-run averages in a stable system: L = lambda times W, where L is the average number of jobs in the system, lambda is the average arrival rate, and W is the average time a job spends in the system. Use consistent boundaries and time units. For a stable service at 50 requests per second and a mean time in the system of 0.2 seconds, the average number in the system is 10. This is an average, not a concurrency cap or a percentile guarantee.

title: Python asyncio cooperative scheduling
text: An asyncio event loop uses cooperative scheduling: it runs one Task at a time. When a task awaits an unfinished Future, the task is suspended and the loop can run other tasks, callbacks, or I/O. Calling blocking synchronous code directly in the event-loop thread blocks that thread and delays other tasks. An await expression does not by itself guarantee a switch if the awaited operation is already complete.

title: Python threads and the CPython GIL
text: In a conventional CPython build with the GIL enabled, only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time. Threads can still be useful for overlapping I/O. CPU-bound pure Python work generally does not gain parallel bytecode execution from additional threads in that build; multiprocessing is an alternative. Free-threaded CPython builds can disable the GIL, so claims about this constraint must state the build assumption.

title: Python thread locks and shared state
text: A threading.Lock provides mutual exclusion: once acquired, another acquire blocks until it is released, unless nonblocking or timed behavior was requested. A lock can protect a critical section that reads and updates shared state. A multi-step read-modify-write algorithm should not be assumed safe merely because the interpreter has a GIL. Using the same lock around the complete critical section coordinates cooperating threads.

title: Python asyncio TaskGroup failures
text: An asyncio.TaskGroup is an asynchronous context manager that waits for its tasks when the context exits. The first child failure with an exception other than asyncio.CancelledError cancels the group's remaining tasks; the group waits for them to finish. Non-cancellation exceptions are then combined into an ExceptionGroup or BaseExceptionGroup, with special handling for KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit. Coroutines should use finally for cleanup and generally propagate cancellation.

title: SQL NULL and comparisons
text: In PostgreSQL, ordinary comparisons such as value = NULL yield null (unknown), not true or false. Use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL to test nullness. A WHERE clause retains rows for which its condition is true, excluding false and unknown. IS DISTINCT FROM treats null as a comparable value for a null-safe difference test; IS NOT DISTINCT FROM provides the corresponding equality-like test.

title: SQL inner and left joins
text: An inner join produces rows for matches satisfying its join condition. A left outer join also preserves every left-side row: when no right-side match exists, right-side columns are filled with nulls. A right-table filter applied in WHERE after a left join can remove these null-extended rows. Placing a qualifying right-side condition in ON instead changes matching while retaining unmatched left rows.

title: SQL aggregate count variants
text: In PostgreSQL, count(*) counts all input rows. count(expression) counts input rows where the expression is not null. count(DISTINCT expression) counts distinct non-null values. For rows whose value column is 7, 7, and NULL, count(*) is 3, count(value) is 2, and count(DISTINCT value) is 1. These aggregates answer different questions about rows and values.

title: SQL transactions and rollback
text: A PostgreSQL transaction groups statements into a single unit: BEGIN starts an explicit transaction block, COMMIT makes the transaction's changes permanent, and ROLLBACK cancels its uncommitted changes. If no explicit transaction block is started, each successful statement runs in its own transaction. A savepoint inside a transaction allows rollback of work after that savepoint while preserving earlier work in the transaction.

title: Git commits and branch references
text: A Git commit records a snapshot through a tree, parent commit identifiers, author and committer information, and a message. A branch name is a movable reference to a commit; committing while on that branch advances its reference. HEAD normally names the current branch, but in detached HEAD state it refers directly to a commit. A branch is not a separate copied directory of project files.

title: Git merge and rebase

Rebasing commits that others have based work on rewrites shared history and requires coordination.

title: Git revert and reset
text: git revert records new commits that reverse changes introduced by selected existing commits; the original commits remain in history. While on a branch, git reset moves its tip to a specified commit, with its mode controlling effects on the index and working tree. --soft leaves the index and working tree unchanged. --mixed resets the index but leaves the working tree. --hard resets both and can discard uncommitted changes. Revert is commonly appropriate for undoing a commit already shared with others.

title: Git restore and the staging area

title: RabbitMQ consumer acknowledgements
text: A RabbitMQ consumer acknowledgement tells the broker that a delivery has been processed and can be removed. With manual acknowledgements, a delivery left unacknowledged when its channel or connection closes can be requeued and redelivered. A consumer can finish an external side effect and lose its connection before the acknowledgement is received, so redelivery may repeat work. At-least-once delivery therefore requires consumers to tolerate possible duplicates.

title: Idempotent message processing
text: An idempotent consumer makes repeated processing of the same message produce the same intended business effect as processing it once. One common design uses a stable message or business-operation identifier and stores a processed-identifier record with the business update in the same database transaction. If the deduplication record and business update are separate non-atomic operations, a crash between them can cause lost effects or duplicates. This is application behavior, not a guarantee that a broker physically delivers only once.

title: RabbitMQ publisher confirms versus consumer acknowledgements
text: RabbitMQ publisher confirms and consumer acknowledgements solve separate problems. A publisher confirm informs the publishing connection about the broker's handling of its published message. A consumer acknowledgement informs the broker about a consumer's processing of a delivery. A publisher confirm does not establish that a consumer has completed the business operation; consumer acknowledgements do not confirm publication to the publisher.

title: RabbitMQ prefetch and unacknowledged deliveries
text: With manual consumer acknowledgements, RabbitMQ prefetch limits how many delivered messages may remain unacknowledged. For a consumer with prefetch count 5, once five deliveries are outstanding the broker stops sending more to that consumer until acknowledgements free capacity. A prefetch count of zero means no such limit. Prefetch limits in-flight delivery count; it does not itself promise a messages-per-second processing rate.

title: DNS positive-answer TTL
text: A DNS resource record's TTL is a time-to-live value in seconds that limits how long the record may be cached before it must be discarded or refreshed. A caching resolver reduces the remaining TTL as cached data ages. A TTL of zero means the data should be used only for the transaction in progress and not cached for later use. A record's TTL is not a promise that every resolver immediately sees a changed authoritative value.

title: TCP byte-stream delivery
text: TCP provides a reliable, in-order byte-stream service between endpoints. It does not preserve application message boundaries: one send may be read in pieces, and bytes from multiple sends may be returned together. An application that needs distinct messages must define framing, such as a length prefix or delimiter. Ordered byte delivery does not by itself show that the receiving application completed a business operation.

title: UDP datagram delivery
text: UDP carries individual datagrams with message boundaries. UDP itself does not guarantee delivery, duplicate protection, or ordering. Applications that need those properties must supply suitable behavior or use another transport. The existence of datagram boundaries does not mean every datagram will reach the receiver or that network fragmentation cannot occur.

title: DNS negative caching
text: DNS negative caching can store an answer that a name does not exist (NXDOMAIN) or that the requested type has no data. An authoritative negative answer includes an SOA record used to determine its negative caching lifetime. Under RFC 2308, that lifetime is the smaller of the SOA record's TTL and its MINIMUM field. A negative cache entry expires after its TTL; a single NXDOMAIN response does not prove a name can never exist later.
